abstract: Abstract Autonomous mobile agents powered by multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong capabilities in task planning and UI navigation. However, existing benchmarks evaluate agents almost exclusively in synthetic desktop emulators, masking the physical constraints that govern real-world deployment on resource-constrained devices: battery drain, thermal throttling, dynamic power regimes, and end-to-end latency over wireless networks. To bridge this gap, we introduce BeYond The Emulator (BYTE), an open benchmarking framework that connects physical Android smartphones directly to foundation models using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). BYTE separates agent perception and action from out-of-band task evaluation, while a lightweight on-device service collects real-time battery, power, and thermal metrics on mobile devices over wireless ADB. Evaluating both cloud-offloaded and on-device foundation models on physical hardware uncovers deployment constraints that synthetic emulators fundamentally cannot capture: dynamic power envelopes, sustained thermal accumulation under inference, and non-linear energy scaling across task complexity and compute localities. These findings demonstrate that grounding evaluation in physical device telemetry is essential for assessing foundation model readiness under real-world resource constraints. Abstract ASR bias research is largely English-focused and the mechanisms underlying performance disparities remain poorly understood. We address both gaps for Spanish and French. Using a 20-hour, gender-balanced corpus (the first for these languages designed for dialect bias analysis, with country-level stratification and manual transcripts preserving dialectal features), we benchmark seven models and find non-uniform disparities: models favor European varieties in French, while Spanish reveals unexpected patterns with Dominican outperforming Peninsular and with Chilean showing the highest error rates. Lexical analysis links failures to morphosyntactic "correction" and regional discourse markers; acoustic analysis shows that speaker embeddings encode dialect information; a diagnostic fine-tuning experiment localizes these errors to the decoder. Together, these results demonstrate that ASR errors systematically reflect linguistic distance from training distributions. Abstract We present a polynomial-time algorithm for computing an optimal committee of size $k$ under any given Thiele voting rule for elections on the Voter Interval domain (i.e., voters can be ordered so that each candidate is approved by a contiguous block of voters). Our result extends to the Generalized Thiele rule, in which each voter has an individual weight (scoring) sequence. This resolves a 10-year-old open problem that was originally posed for Proportional Approval Voting and later extended to every Thiele rule. Our main technical ingredient is a new structural result---a concavity theorem for families of intervals. It shows that, given two solutions of different sizes, one can construct a solution of any intermediate size whose score is at least the corresponding linear interpolation of the two scores. As a consequence, on Voter Interval profiles the optimal total Thiele score is a concave function of the committee size. We exploit this concavity within an optimization framework based on a Lagrangian relaxation of a natural integer linear program formulation, obtained by moving the cardinality constraint into the objective. On Voter Interval profiles, the resulting constraint matrix is totally unimodular, so it can be solved in polynomial time. Our main algorithm and its proof were obtained via human--AI collaboration. In particular, a slightly simplified version of the main structural theorem used by the algorithm was obtained in a single call to Gemini Deep Think. Abstract We prove that deg(f) = O~(rdeg(f)) for every Boolean function f, where deg(f) is the degree of f and rdeg(f) is the rational degree of f. This resolves the second of the three open problems stated by Nisan and Szegedy, and attributed to Fortnow, in 1994. Abstract Bidirectional (right-to-left, RTL) layout defects arise when interfaces authored with physical directional CSS (margin-left, border-left, text-align:left) are rendered under dir="rtl" without being mirrored. Accessibility engines (axe-core), actionability engines (Playwright), and even Stylelint's current core logical-property rule systematically fail to localise these defects. We present runtime structural invariants, a zero-golden mode over computed style and geometry, and a bidi-conservative differential mode — that catch them in a headless browser. On a held-out benchmark of 14 real RTL bugs reconstructed from dated fix commits in Bootstrap and Material Components Web, the detector recovers 13/14 (2 via zero-golden, 11 via the differential mode), with no false alarm on any patched version; on genuinely real historical compiled CSS it catches 1 of 2 attempted, using the actual committed bootstrap.rtl.css. On 16 negative LTR-island cases (8 hard) it reports 0 false positives, and both modes report 0 false positives on 43 unmodified real components across four design systems and three RTL architectures (rule-of-three 95% upper bound ≤ 7%). It surfaced a real directional defect : a physical text-align:left in .menu-list in the current Bulma 1.0.4. By contrast, Stylelint's core rule emits an identical 1744 warnings on Bootstrap's LTR and correct-RTL builds, pseudo-localisation detects none of the mirroring bugs, and a naive pixel mirror-and-diff reaches only F1 0.87 with a test-set-tuned threshold, whereas the differential needs none. We find the two modes complementary and scope this paper to detection; repair is future work. Abstract Content moderation compresses a graded, contested human judgment into a binary act (leave up / take down) over billions of items, at a scale where running a frontier LLM on every post is uneconomical. A new class of frozen "System One" models returns typed, calibrated decisions instead of text at ~$0.000025 per call and ~100 ms. We run the first independent audit of one such model on 142,658 human-labeled comments, and benchmark it against 14 frontier reasoning models (the GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini 3, and Grok families) on a shared probe set. Two findings stand out. First, the cheap model is accuracy-competitive: its zero-shot classification AUROC (0.83) is not statistically separable (paired bootstrap, n=56; a failure to reject parity, not proof of equivalence) from 13 of the 14 frontier systems while costing 1–3 orders of magnitude less, and it is no worse calibrated than several of them. Second, "confidence" conflates two uncertainties that come apart: human disagreement (where annotators split on satire and coded language) and decision risk (where the automatic action is costly-wrong). Under an asymmetric moderation loss these call for opposite escalation signals, so no single confidence number serves both. Because the model prices extra questions at nearly zero, decomposing the judgment into parallel sub-questions and reading their spread recovers a human-disagreement signal that the model's native confidence misses—but this remedy is specific: it helps the weakest, disagreement-blind models and only when the decomposition aligns with the sources of disagreement; a specialist toxicity model and the strongest LLMs do not need it, and the effect is distribution-sensitive. We release the instrument, the cached runs, and the analysis.
